title: New issue of Econ Journal Watch - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: The September 2026 Econ Journal Watch issue challenges prominent results: corrected 'China shock' estimates show no labor-market harm, post-SFFA Black enrollment predictions failed, Fama-French and momentum factors suffered structural breaks, and chatbots proved fallible at validating math-econ proofs.

insights.claim: Joseph Francis argues that when the Borusyak et al. (2022) corrections are fully applied to Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013), the estimated harm of Chinese imports to US unemployment, labor force participation, wages and household incomes disappears.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Undercuts a key empirical pillar for tariff and protectionist policy toward China.
insights.quote: the harm of Chinese imports to unemployment, labor force participation, wages, and household incomes disappear

insights.claim: Francis presents the China shock literature as an example of how the 'credibility revolution' still leaves 'the con in econometrics'.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Prominent quasi-experimental findings used in policy may be fragile.

insights.claim: Michael O'Connor argues momentum's demise around 2003, and the demise of the size (market cap) and book-to-market (value) factors about a decade later, represent a structural break or regime change rather than temporary underperformance.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Directly relevant to quant/factor allocations: if the break is real, historical factor premia should not be expected to return.
insights.locator: The fall of Fama-French and momentum factors

insights.claim: Before SFFA v. Harvard (June 2023) banned race-based admissions, 33 selective colleges forecast Black enrollment declines of 50-70%, and David Card estimated Harvard's admitted Black share would fall from 14% to 6%; three years on, David Kane reports these predictions did not come close to true.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Expert institutional forecasts of policy impacts can be badly wrong — a caution for consensus-driven predictions.
insights.quote: Thirty-three selective colleges forecast Black enrollment declines of 50 to 70 percent.
insights.locator: The predictions did not come true

insights.claim: Alexis Akira Toda tested chatbots on finding errors in four published mathematical-economics papers: they produced false positives by endorsing flawed proofs, with ChatGPT Pro performing best, Claude middling and Gemini worst.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Relative LLM performance on rigorous reasoning tasks differs; none are yet reliable validators.
insights.quote: ChatGPT Pro performed best, Claude was middling, and Gemini worst.

insights.claim: Because corrections of the original errors had already been published, chatbot successes may reflect canvassing published commentary rather than reasoning, while the false positives prove the chatbots fallible either way.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Benchmark contamination can overstate LLM reasoning ability.
insights.quote: Since the chatbots generated false positives, however, we know that they are fallible one way or another.

insights.claim: Kenneth Judd and Karl Schmedders argue Jesús Fernández-Villaverde overstates the novelty of neural-network 'deep learning' solvers, which belong to the family of projection and weighted-residual solvers.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Deep learning in economics may be less revolutionary than claimed.

insights.claim: Michael Weissman criticizes Worobey et al. in Science, arguing several lines of evidence suggest SARS-CoV-2 was introduced to humans earlier and elsewhere than the Huanan Seafood Market.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Keeps the COVID-origins debate open, with geopolitical implications for China.

insights.claim: Jens Hansen's history of 1939-1945 Danish housing policy finds rent control and other housing regulation wrought great hardship with no discernible benefits, exemplifying the intervention dynamic.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Historical evidence against rent control relevant to current housing policy debates.
insights.quote: The interventions have wrought great hardship and no discernible benefits.

insights.claim: John Levendis argues that, contrary to the UN Digital Public Goods Alliance framework, evidence from Sri Lanka and Norway Covid-19 surveillance tools shows local professionals cooperated voluntarily and community innovation preceded WHO guidance.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Bottom-up open-source development may outperform top-down multilateral frameworks.
insights.quote: community innovation preceded WHO guidance, not the reverse
insights.locator: How are so-called digital public goods provided?

insights.claim: The issue hosts a symposium on Gregory Clark's forthcoming book To Have and Have Not: The Determinants of Social Status in England, 1600-2026, the third in his trilogy on genetics and social mobility, with comments from Plomin, Charles Murray and others.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Persistent-status research informs long-run views on inequality and mobility.
